title: The Name on the Slate
passages:
The sky over the Kettle went the color of a wet coin an hour before noon, and the season bell up on the arcology's high tower started its slow count, one strike every ten seconds, the way it did when a channel was about to close and everybody's unfinished business became everybody's emergency. Wren had the chart-space hatch propped open to let the heat out, which also let the rain in sideways, and she worked with one shoulder hunched against it.

The slate sat on her bench in a puddle of its own rust. A slate is the recorder a diver clips to the chest strap of his harness: it logs his voice and his depth, hour on hour, so that a topside tech can rebuild a dive that nobody came up to describe. This one had gone into Mercy General's flooded stairwell fourteen months ago with Ivo Salas strapped inside the same harness, and it had come out of the pocket at forty-two meters crusted the green-gray of a hull plate.

"Give it here." Bayo leaned in the hatchway, dry, which was more than the rest of them could manage. "I've a hand for old gear."

"You've a hand for old gear the way you've got a berth," Dey said, from the deck where he was sitting with his back against the bench leg, breathing on his own lungs, no scrubber on his chest, because Teo had that. "Warm. And brief."

"I'll take warm."

Wren didn't look up. She had the case cracked and a wire brush going along the contact strip, the little copper comb that carries the charge out of the cell and into the log. Salt gets into everything. Salt gets into a cell and eats it from the inside until what's left is a brick with delusions.

"Talk to me," Salas said. He was standing at her shoulder with his arms folded, a big man gone careful in his movements, watching a piece of his own year get scraped clean. "Is it holding anything?"

"It's fourteen months in seawater. It's holding rust." She flicked rust onto the deck. "Cell's supposed to be flat. Dead as a doornail. That's the whole design — no charge, no log, no ghosts, so nobody spends a week listening to a drowned man's last shift."

"That's considerate of it," Bayo said.

"That's *law*, is what that is." She thumbed the cell free, wiped the contacts down with a rag that had stopped being a rag years ago, and seated it again. "Don't lean on my bench."

In the corner Nia had folded herself down beside the crate where Teo slept with his mouth open, and she was turning his berth-card over and over in her fist — berth four-oh-eight, the arcology's own stock, stamped and paid — like a woman checking a coin she already knew was good. Outside, the bell counted. Inside, the reader waited: a steel box bolted to the bench with a slot in the front and a spool behind glass, a cradle, the thing that plays back what went down with a diver so the top of the world can hear it.

Wren closed the slate into the slot, wiped her hands, and reached for the switch.

The charge gauge on the cradle face was a strip of nine little windows, and it was dark, and it stayed dark for as long as it took her to breathe twice. Then the first window went amber.

Then the second.

"It's reading a charge," she said.

"Good," said Bayo.

"No." Wren sat back. In fourteen months of salt water that cell should have been a stone, and a stone does not have three windows and climbing. Behind the glass, unasked, with nobody's thumb on anything, the spool began to turn.

"Leave it," Wren said, and took her hand off the switch.

The cradle had a speaker grille the size of a saucer, and what came out of it first was water. Not the sea outside, hammering the deck plates — a slower sound, a drip with a rhythm to it, landing somewhere close to the microphone. Then a valve cracked, a short hard hiss, the sound of a man opening his air for a second and shutting it again to make it last. Then Ivo Salas, fourteen months dead, said something.

His voice came out thin and wet, sanded down to almost nothing, a man talking around a mouthful of coins. Two syllables. He said them and stopped, and the drip went on, and he said them again.

"Again," Dey said. He'd come up onto his knees without seeming to decide to.

The spool ran. *Ma —* and then the second part, soft on both ends, a word you'd call across water to somebody you couldn't see yet.

The depth line under the grille read forty-one point six meters. The clock read three hours and eleven minutes into a shift that, as far as the arcology's book was concerned, had ended when the hospital went under.

"Turn it off," Bayo said, and nobody did.

It said the name nine times while they stood there. Wren counted, because counting was what her hands did when the rest of her had stopped. Between each one: the drip, the hiss, and under all of it, so far down in the mix that it might have been the boat's own hull, a bell.

Salas hadn't moved. His arms had come unfolded and he had one hand flat on her bench, in the rust puddle, not seeming to notice.

"That's it," he said.

"That's what?"

"That's the one." He straightened up. He was a big man and the chart-space was not, and he took his hand off the bench and looked at the shape his fingers had left in the rust like it belonged to somebody else. "Every slack water. The Caller gives it back to me. My own voice, my own throat, saying that, and I stand there like a fool waiting for the rest of the sentence."

Wren turned the gain down until the drip was all that was left. "You've heard this before. This exact recording."

"I've heard the word. Not the tape." He nodded at the cradle, and his jaw worked. "I couldn't hang a face on it. Still can't. There's a hole where the face goes."

"Say it," Dey said.

Salas said it. In the room, in his own mouth, with air in it, it came out flatter and older and much too ordinary, and Wren watched four people fail to recognize it.

"Nobody?" Bayo said. "Not one of you? Big man, fourteen months in the dark, saying a name like a prayer — and no one's mother, no one's sister?"

"I don't know my own middle name some days," Salas said. "Don't ask me for a roster."

Nia hadn't moved out of the corner. Wren was aware of her the way you're aware of a line under load, something in the room holding more than it looked like it could hold.

The fourth window on the charge gauge went amber.

"Cell's supposed to be a brick," Wren said. "That's the law, that's the *design* — you go down, you come up, you hand me the slate, and there's nothing in it but the shift you already told me about." She wiped her palms on her thighs. "This thing has fourteen months of tape left on it and a charge to run it, and I want somebody to explain to me how, because I can't."

Outside, the season bell struck, and the rain came across the hatch in a fistful.

Behind the glass the spool kept turning, patient, going back down into the hours.

PASSAGE END

She put her thumb on the scrub wheel.

It sat under the cradle glass, a brass knob knurled like the edge of a coin, and it did what its name said — dragged you through a log by hand without playing it, hour on hour, the way you'd walk a finger down a column of numbers hunting the one that didn't belong. Wren turned it back slow and watched the depth line climb out of forty-one meters. Forty. Thirty-nine. She let it run and caught it.

"Find me the rest of the sentence," Salas said. "I want the words after it."

"Give me a minute. I want the shape of the whole thing first."

She dragged, and the spool behind the glass stuttered backward through a year of dark, the little speaker clicking as it skipped whole hours — a dry tick, a clock learning to stutter. Every sound on the tape had a number pinned to it. The slate doesn't only keep a diver's voice; it keeps his air against the scrubber cycle, one cycle to a breath, the rhythm of a bottle being emptied and cleaned and handed back, so a tech topside can lay a man's words over exactly how much of him was left to spend. Wren had rebuilt a hundred dives off those numbers. She knew what a man wasting air looked like: the gauge bleeding down in a long even slope, all the way to nothing.

This wasn't that.

She found the name at eleven hours in. Dragged on. Found it again at eleven and forty. Again at twelve. She went faster, thumb walking the wheel, and the name came up, and came up, and came up — the same two syllables, soft at both ends, patient as the drip behind it.

"Watch the air-gauge for me," she said. "That needle under the depth line. Tell me what it does when it says the word."

Bayo leaned in, close enough that she could smell the rain still on him. "Flat," he said. "Flat, flat — there. It jumps. Up hard, then straight back down."

"Keep watching."

"Again." A pause. "It says the word, the needle jumps, and they go quiet together."

Wren let the spool run at speed, thumb light on the brass, and the name went past so fast it stopped being a word and became weather — the same soft sound over and over, and under each one the needle flicked up and fell, up and fell.

"That's not waste," she said. "Waste is a slope. That's a *draw*. Somebody cracks the bottle open on purpose, gives the air out instead of breathing it in, and for one second the gauge jumps because there's a hole in the line where it's all going." She stopped the wheel. Her hand had gone flat on the bench, in the rust, the way Salas's had. "That's him opening his valve for somebody. Every time he says her name, he's handing air out into the dark."

The bell struck outside, and this time nobody counted it.

Wren looked at the tape counter and did the arithmetic she didn't want to do — a bottle is so many breaths, a breath is a cycle, a year is so many cycles — and the numbers came out wrong. Came out impossible. A man cannot crack his bottle hundreds of times and still be breathing at the end of it.

Unless.

She took her hand off the wheel and left it there, not touching anything, while the spool kept turning.

"Unless he wasn't breathing it," Wren said.

Bayo was still bent over the gauge, one finger tapping the glass in time. "Three seconds between them, most times. Four when he's slow about it. Crack, name, hiss, and go again." He straightened. "Then a long quiet — hours of it, some stretches — and it starts up again. Same beat, all the way down. It's the count you keep coming the Stair, so you know how much stair you've left."

"I don't care about your beat," Dey said. He'd gotten up onto his feet, which for a man breathing on his own lungs these days was not nothing. "I care about the hole in the line. You keep saying *somebody.* Somebody at forty-two meters. Somebody he cracks his bottle for." He turned on Salas. "That run was a sealed pocket. A pharmacy lock. A *crate* job. There was nobody down there to hand air to. So who was it, old man?"

Salas didn't answer. He was looking at the shape his hand had left in the rust as if it might have changed while nobody watched.

"A sealed pocket holds air," Wren said. "Trapped. A whole room of it caught under a floor that's turned over, no way out but the one you came in by. That's the thing that keeps a man going when his bottle's dry. It's why he's standing in my chart-space and not written down as a body." She tapped the glass. "He was living on the room. And the bottle he wasn't breathing — that one he was handing out."

The drip landed. The valve hissed.

"Every one of these," she said, "he cracks the valve and gives the room's spare to somebody who didn't have a room. A diver doesn't crack his bottle into the dark for fun. You do it once, maybe, for a partner whose line's fouled, and count yourself lucky you had it to give. You don't do it hundreds of times. Not for a partner." She looked up. "You do it for somebody you keep going back to. That's not a rescue. That's a shift. A man spending his own hours to sit in the dark and make sure somebody else wakes up."

Nobody had a joke for that. Even Bayo.

"I fix slates," she went on, before anyone could ask the next thing. "Was the whole of my job. A diver comes up wrong, I find the hour that broke him and file it smooth so his people get him back easy. I was good at it." A short breath, not quite a laugh. "I stopped a season back — the day I put Sol's own hour back in her head and swore I was done shaving people clean. A slate I'd edited was a slate I'd lied in, and I got sick of my own hand doing that to folks."

"So you know it's true," Dey said. "This one."

"The slate doesn't lie. It can't. It knows two things — the voice and the air — and it writes both down without asking anybody's leave. It rode on his chest fourteen months and took down every one of these." She let the spool run; the name came around, and the needle jumped and fell with it. "So it's not a ghost, and it's not a bad cell. There was a person down there, breathing his air, the whole time." She looked at Salas, at the hole where his memory of the face should be. "And he can't tell you who."

Up on the high tower the season bell struck, and nobody counted it, and behind the glass the name came around again.

The name came around one more time and Wren let it, and watched Nia instead of the gauge.

The girl had gone the kind of still you learn in a tower where the first rule is don't be the one anybody notices. A year of running a cold-box by hand will do that. She sat with her back against the crate, Teo's mouth open beside her, the berth-card folded so far into her fist that the stamped edge had pressed a white line across her palm. She wasn't looking at the cradle. She was looking at the grille — that saucer of little holes the voice came out of — the way you look at a door somebody is about to come through.

"Nia," Wren said. "You know that name."

Nothing. The drip landed. The valve hissed.

"Hey," Dey said. "You've gone the color of the deck plates."

"Leave her be," Salas said.

"I'm not touching her. I'm *asking* her."

"Play it again," Nia said.

Wren looked at Bayo. Bayo shrugged, which from Bayo was practically a notarized document. She backed the brass wheel two teeth and let it run.

*Ma—* and the soft second part, and the hiss.

Nia's eyes were shut. Her lips moved along with it, no sound, the way you do in a room where somebody else is praying and you don't want to be caught not knowing the words.

"Again."

Wren ran it again.

"Again."

"Nia—"

"*Again.*" The fifth window on the charge gauge went amber while she said it.

The third time. The fourth. On the fifth Nia opened her eyes and said the two syllables out loud in her own voice — a kid's voice, with air behind it, pitched to carry across a flooded ward to somebody you couldn't see yet. It didn't sound like the tape at all. That was the thing. The tape was a man sanded down to nothing, spending what he had left to keep saying a woman's name into the dark.

"Mara," Nia said. "Mara Vos." She held it out the way you'd hand somebody something breakable, and she didn't look at any of them when she did it. "That's my mother's name."

The bell struck up on the high tower. Nobody counted.

"Well," Bayo said, into that, "that's better than a sister—"

"Bayo." Wren didn't raise her voice.

"I'm only saying it's better."

Dey had both hands on the bench edge, leaning in, and for once he wasn't the one talking too fast. Salas hadn't moved at all. Behind the glass the spool kept turning, patient, going back down into the hours, and the name came up out of the grille again in a dead man's borrowed throat while his face did nothing, because there was nothing behind it to do anything with.

Nia got up. She put Teo's card in her shirt, buttoned it, and stood there with her arms at her sides, four feet of girl in a chart-space full of divers, looking at the grille like it owed her fourteen months.

"How does a man I never met know my mother's name?"

Nobody answered her, because nobody in the chart-space had the answer, and the only person who might have was standing in it with a hole where the answer went.

"I can do it," Dey said. "He doesn't know her. That's the trouble with him. That's the trouble with the whole crew."

"Says the man who gave his scrubber to a kid and then went down anyway to prove a point," Bayo said.

"That's not the same."

"It's the same, only you got to keep your face."

"Both of you, off my deck," Wren said, without heat, and kept her thumb on the brass wheel.

Salas hadn't looked away from Nia. "I never met your mother," he said. "I'll say that to anybody you want, and I'll say it sorry, because it's true and it doesn't help you." He rubbed his palm, and the rust on it had dried to the color of an old scar. "Fourteen months I've had her name in my mouth and no face to hang it on. You'd think a man would be glad to have somebody walk in and fill the gap."

Nia crossed the chart-space. She was four feet of girl and she came across the deck plates like the deck owed her, and she took his hand — the big one, the one with the print in it — and turned it over and looked at the palm the way Wren looked at a contact strip.

"Something," she said. "Not the name. Something about her."

Salas reached. It took him a while, and the drip landed twice in it.

"Hair," he said. "Short. Cut ragged, with a knife, not scissors. You can see where it steps, there, above the ear."

Nia's grip tightened on his hand hard enough that Wren saw the tendons stand up in her wrist.

"I cut that," Nia said. "In the ward. The scissors had rusted shut so I used the knife off her tray."

"Careful," Wren said, and both of them looked at her. She tapped the cradle face, the nine little windows, five of them amber. "Every time that spool runs, it costs a window. That's not a setting, it's the cell — the charge in there is what's left of fourteen months, and it doesn't come back, not off the boat's line, not off anything. Five gone. Four left. When they're dark that slate is a brick again forever, and everything your mother said in the dark goes with it."

"So don't spend one on my hair," Dey said.

"I didn't spend one. Dragging's free. It's playing that eats it." Wren took her thumb off the wheel. "Four plays. Spend them like breaths, because that's what they are."

Nia let go of Salas's hand. "What else."

"She sang," Salas said.

The rain came across the hatch. The bell struck, and this time Wren counted it, because her hands needed somewhere to be.

"No," Nia said.

"Nia—"

"She never sang." The girl's voice didn't rise. That was the worst of it; she said it the way you'd read a gauge. "Not once, not for us, not ever. Singing is air. She counted air like it was blood, she counted it out loud so Teo would learn to, and she wouldn't have wasted a mouthful on a song if the tower was on fire." She was still holding Teo's berth-card through her shirt, flat against her chest. "You've got a woman in your head who wastes air. That's not her. That's not anybody I ever lived with."

Nobody said anything for long enough that the drip got loud.

"Then one of you is wrong about her," Nia said, "and I'm not going to find out which standing in a boat." She buttoned her shirt over the card, twice, the second button going into the wrong hole, and left it wrong. "Play it again. Play it until he gets her right."

Wren looked at the four amber windows, and did the arithmetic, and didn't say the answer out loud.
